To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs.

Researchers have observed that extremely long, thin polymer bristles that are in a state of molecular disarray often exhibit areas closer to their tips where interactions are reduced or minimized, even with changes in surface properties or temperature. A mathematical model, which accounts for fluctuations in polymer chains, has been applied to determine the characteristics of these less interactive edge regions for polymer bristles of varying shapes, like lines, curves, and branches, and demonstrates that the less interactive edge regions are always located towards the bristle's end and that the length of these regions increases as the bristle's length increases. Furthermore, compared to linear bristles of an identical total length, the less interactive edge regions of branched bristles are found to be smaller in size. This research also explores how these less interactive edge regions evolve over time and provides mathematical equations that can be used for bristles of different shapes and sizes.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when its vertex set can be distinguished uniquely by a set of distances, using a specific metric dimension. However, for many graphs, this high standard of identification isn't necessary or useful. Therefore, we introduce a new, less stringent standard of identification - a graph G is called SD-identifiable if its vertex set can be distinguished using a reduced metric dimension. We then examine properties of SD-identifiable graphs and establish connections between them and graphs with a particular type of vertex identification property.

Researchers have developed a method for enhancing all-sky maps using Fermi-LAT data by implementing machine learning techniques. All-sky maps serve a critical function in identifying and locating gamma-ray sources across the sky. Despite extensive observation, Fermi-LAT's sensitivity and sensitivity to varying sources remain limitations. A comparison of the proposed method to existing approaches using real data from Fermi-LAT has been performed, demonstrating improvements in source detection and reducing false positives by approximately 10%. The application of machine learning models to historical data from Fermi-LAT has also been tested, highlighting over a hundred variable sources with intense emission over a duration of nearly a decade. These sources were subsequently validated using satellite imagery and emission patterns from various celestial objects, further highlighting the utility of this method in identifying variable sources.

In a serial dictatorship where one individual makes consecutive decisions for the benefit of different people, the person with the most influence will always benefit the most. This knowledge is used to examine the possibility of improving a state of affairs in a scenario where one person has complete control over a sequence of decisions. More specifically, we investigate if it's possible to create a social welfare that ranks all possible states of affairs in a particular order, with the most desirable being the state of a single-person dictatorship, the next most desirable being a two-person dictatorship, and so on, with the least desirable being a state of complete uncertainty. This inquiry leads us to identify a new class of welfare functions called enhancing over dictatorships, and we discover that these functions share similar characteristics with standard extensions of a welfare function that hold in a independent and identical distribution setting.

We developed a method for detecting binary asteroids within the solar system by utilizing images from the Pan-STARRS1 telescope. By analyzing a comprehensive database of 1.5 million high-quality images spanning nearly a decade, we were able to identify 89 candidate binary asteroids that have distinct orbital periods between 0.1 days and 60 days. Each detection met the stringent criteria of displaying a consistent illumination pattern across multiple images, indicating a stable three-body configuration. Furthermore, we were able to determine the shape parameters of potential syntheses for each binary asteroid candidate by applying an advanced modeling technique that leverages the inherent properties of their light curves. Notably, the vast majority, approximately 95%, of our detected binary candidates were composed of asteroids with sizes ranging from 100 meters to 2 kilometers, suggesting that binaries may be prevalent among small asteroids.

In statistics and machine learning, partial linear regression refers to a method that combines elements of linear and non-parametric regression to analyze data with the presence of a continuous controlling variable. We have developed an original approach to estimate the parameters in a one-dimensional partial linear regression model and subsequently applied this estimation to extract the parameters of a multi-dimensional partial linear regression model. The multi-dimensional model incorporates network data and peer influences to enhance the quality of the estimates. We have conducted extensive simulations to evaluate the performance of our proposed method and compared it to alternative approaches, such as the local quadratic spline estimator and the isotonic estimator. Our results show that the proposed method performs well across various scenarios and data types. We have also analyzed real world data sets involving network data and peer influences to demonstrate the practical applications of the method.

This study extends the Leibniz Rule to both basic and classical Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integrals and derivatives. If we denote the variable-order fractional integrals and derivatives as $I^{\Sigma}(f(x))$ and $I^{\Sigma}(f(x))$, respectively, then the extended Leibniz rules are given by $I^{\Sigma}_{a}(f(x)) = \int_{a}^{x} \frac{\Gamma(s+1)\Gamma(Q(x)-s)}{\Gamma(Q(x))}\cdot f(t)dt$ and $\frac{d^{\Sigma}_{a}f(x)}{dx^{\Sigma}_{a}} = \frac{\Gamma(Q(x))}{\Gamma(1)\Gamma(Q(x)-1)}\cdot f(x)$.

On-line group interactions like Dungeons and Dragons allow players to connect with their friends through immersive role-playing activities, despite being physically distant from one another. However, guiding a team of players through such an engaging story requires a high degree of storytelling expertise, making it challenging for individuals to take on this role without extensive training. To overcome this difficulty, we suggest a new approach, drawing from artificial intelligence and computer-mediated communication principles. In this approach, the dungeon master is seen as a supervisor who can learn from players' interactions, developing unique storytelling skills. To demonstrate how this can happen, we created a synthetic environment where a intelligent agent learns to guide players through a fantasy world by interpreting verbal instructions. This agent's goal is to lead the players to enchanted islands while confronting obstacles like treacherous weather conditions. To achieve this, we established a clear language rule that enables the agent to understand and respond to the players' statements, incorporating elements of game state, character actions, and dialogue history. As a result, the agent's direction methods become more sophisticated over time, allowing it to successfully complete the quest at an impressive rate of over 90%. Notably, this achievement occurs in the absence of any pre-programmed intentions related to the game, illustrating the effectiveness of its supervised learning approach. To facilitate this learning process, we recommend introducing a morale factor that affects the agent's decision-making behavior, further enhancing its ability to navigate complex situations effectively.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their function is being revealed through statistical and computational analyses. Recent studies suggest knots may hinder or refold to protect proteins from denaturation. A new method uses topological characteristics to examine how knotted proteins unfold and re-knit under different forces, demonstrating a link between local bond variations and global knot structures. Specifically, it's shown how knotted proteins form slipknots rather than trefoil knots when subjected to force, and a general pattern of bond alteration preferred by protein knots in three-dimensional space. This research provides a foundation for further investigation into the complex relationship between protein knots and their molecular structures.

Let $\omega$ be a symplectic form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via a non-degenerate change of variables, this note establishes that the mapping class group of the symplectic resolvent $(T^4,\omega)$ is isomorphic to the mapping class group of $(T^4,\omega)$ itself, equivalently speaking it is generically isomorphic to $SE(2,2)$. Additionally, when $\omega$ is rational, the mapping class group is determined to be both finite and explicitly given.

A detailed investigation of the irregular NG theorem is carried out, addressing its fundamental proof and relevant applications in both high-energy physics, specifically in QCD, and in the study of low-lying energy levels in certain nuclear and molecular systems.

Recent advancements in utilizing large language models for counterfactual reasoning have focused primarily on individual alterations. In contrast, our approach, dubbed DISCO, explores the potential of these models to incorporate more comprehensive counterfactual scenarios characterized by multiple phrasal changes. To evaluate the capabilities of these models in this context, we designed a novel task involving a multiple-choice format where counterfactual phrases are presented among valid options. To demonstrate the applicability of our method, we constructed two such datasets incorporating both single and multi-phrasal counterfactual scenarios. Our results show that extremely large language models perform exceptionally well in both single and multi-phrasal scenarios, outperforming smaller models by significant margins. Furthermore, we discovered that these models excel at distinguishing between plausible and unlikely counterfactual scenarios, achieving a 70% accuracy rate with our largest model. Lastly, we analyzed the importance of contextual context in counterfactual reasoning and found it to be negligible in our datasets.

We investigated the epitaxial growth of CoPtHeusler layers on a graphene-sapphire substrate across various temperatures, and identified three distinct epitaxial mechanisms: van der Waals, patch, and migration-controlled edge pinhole epitaxy. The prevalence of these mechanisms was highly dependent on both the temperature and humidity levels, which significantly impacted the crystalline structure and morphology of the CoPtHeusler films. When heated above 700°C in a dry environment, the films exhibited a stress-free state with a hexagonal close-packed structure and a large lattice parameter, corresponding to van der Waals epitaxy. In more humid conditions, or at lower temperatures, the films showed stress and a face-centered cubic structure with a smaller lattice parameter, corresponding to patch or edge pinhole epitaxy respectively. Nevertheless, the electronic and magnetic properties of the CoPtHeusler films remained largely unaffected by the different epitaxial mechanisms. Moreover, by integrating an ultra-thin van der Waals buffer layer of MnS on top of the graphene-sapphire substrate, we were able to achieve dry and annealed conditions with a significant reduction of tension and a more faithful replication of the Heusler films' lattice parameters.

A code is called $Z_pZ_{p^2}$-linear if it is derived from a code with attributes from $Z_pZ_{p^2}$ through the application of permutation matrices and extension matrices. This research focuses on investigating $Z_pZ_{p^2}$-linear error-correcting codes, with a specific interest in their rank, dimension, and null space when correctable errors are considered. It has been demonstrated that $Z_pZ_{p^2}$-linear codes are comparable to GPC codes and that there is a direct relationship between the rank of a $Z_pZ_{p^2}$-linear code and a specific class of GPC codes. Furthermore, this research provides an approach for determining the rank and null space of $Z_pZ_{p^2}$-linear codes utilizing a standard basis of the code's matrix, along with some relevant examples.

In real-world applications, labels often contain additional, related information that can be leveraged to enhance models by providing contextual insight. For example, in text classification, the label "stock market news" could also imply labels like "finance" and "economy," whereas a label like "sports news" would not share these relations. To exploit this phenomenon, we introduce a novel task called contextualized multi-label instance extraction (CMIE), where for each sample, only one relevant label is provided, albeit with the underlying label distribution intact. In effect, CMIE serves as a surrogate for traditional multi-label classification problems. We outline a series of experiments utilizing CMIE to enhance the performance of models for both single-label and multi-label classification tasks. These experiments demonstrate that incorporating CMIE can lead to significant improvements in model accuracy across various domains, including text, where we incorporate CMIE into a BERT-based model, and in image, where we utilize CMIE to augment weakly-supervised object classification.

Quantum field theory involves interpreting physical observables through configurations of fields. In a variational formulation, observables are mapped to symplectic transformations, which in turn are associated with unitary operators on a Hilbert space. A key relationship between configurations and the resulting unitary operators arises from the operator norm, generating the unitary operators from configurations in a systematic way. This connection is the basis for an abstract 2-categorical adjunction, which reflects the underlying relationship between configurations and the associated unitary operators.

The unknown causes of gamma-ray signals observed in many nearby galaxies, emitting rays in the high-energy band, pose a problem for scientists. To explore this phenomenon, we've conducted a thorough analysis of 22 nearby galaxies that are actively emitting polarized radio waves and have accessible data. By applying a new method that takes into account the orientation of magnetic fields, we've identified the likely source of gamma-rays as magnetic fields rather than other factors. Furthermore, we've correlated this effect with the strength of magnetic fields and found that even moderate strengths can produce gamma-rays when combined with fast-spinning black holes. This discovery also provides an alternative explanation for the emergence of very high-energy rays in some sources, suggesting that the process of particle acceleration within these sources is capable of producing extreme effects.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate diagnosis can be impaired by background noise and movement-related distortion during the examination. To address this challenge, an automatic system for heart sound analysis is necessary. Such a system could help medical professionals quickly identify issues like heart valve problems by analyzing recordings from brief, rapid pulse checks. To enhance the effectiveness of such a system in noisy and distorted recordings, this research divides heart sound recordings into distinct categories based on various pulse check movements and identifies patterns of sound associated with these movements. A deep learning approach is used to construct a category system that can tolerate movement-related variations and noise. This results in a robust and practical system that can be utilized in real-world cardiac auscultation applications.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. However, training accurate models using wearable data is challenging due to several issues including small dataset sizes, individual feature sets, and heterogeneity among participants. In a federated learning setting, training models across multiple participants is another difficulty because of security concerns and substantial communication costs. To address these challenges, a new framework called FedHealth is proposed that combines federated learning and knowledge transfer to effectively train models using wearable data. First, the model is trained across participants in a federated learning framework, reducing data heterogeneity. Then, an asymmetric knowledge transfer technique is used to leverage data from a limited number of participants with extensive historical records. To mitigate distributional errors during knowledge transfer, the model is modified to accommodate varying feature sets among participants. The results show that FedHealth achieves a 25% reduction in accuracy compared to a standard federated learning framework and 10% compared to a traditional knowledge transfer framework.

This study explores the connection between a novel mean-upper-cutoff (MUC) method and existing mean-risk optimization approaches, particularly the mean-variance model and its variants, including scalar and vector formulations. Traditional mean-risk models, including the mean-variance model, rely on variance as the risk measure, which can lead to undesirable results in certain situations. Conversely, the MUC framework, by excluding assets with high standard deviation above a designated threshold, provides a more accurate risk representation and thus, in this study, we establish a mathematical framework to equate MUC-optimized portfolios with those optimized using traditional mean-risk approaches.

In large-scale automation environments, software must be managed efficiently
to minimize points of friction and reduce maintenance costs. Despite the benefits
of automation, many organizations struggle to implement reliable, hands-free
software management processes. This struggle is often attributed to the rapid
pace of software development and user feedback. However, experience shows that
even with rapid changes, well-designed automated tools can incorporate new
versions and updates seamlessly. This paper aims to provide practitioners with
guidance on implementing automated software management processes that are resilient
to disruption and require minimal maintenance. By sharing best practices and
lessons learned from successful automated implementations, this paper can help
mitigate common obstacles and facilitate the adoption of hands-free software
management.

This research focuses on a stochastic control problem where the objective function to minimize includes the number of times the control switches, making it a version of a problem with switching costs. Unlike traditional versions, we allow the costs to be unpredictable and depend on the size of the switch. We manage to reduce this variant to a standard stochastic control problem with rewards and penalties, and in the case where the costs are bounded, we are able to obtain a result about the existence of an optimal strategy.

To explore the potential origins of recent anomalous observations in high-energy particle collisions, a theoretical analysis suggests creating two specific types of unusual particles known as leptoquarks through a single high-energy proton-proton collision. This study examines how even or odd (in pairs) these two leptoquarks appear in collisions, depending on an established standard model parameter, at the Large Hadron Collider. Even pairs are more difficult to find than expected based on current experiments, and a proposed search method is presented to evaluate this phenomenon further.

We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies for which data is available for two specific fine structure lines of neutral atomic carbon, and we found that even at the outer reaches of galaxies, the gas is often warmer than expected, potentially indicating external stimulation of the gas. If caused by external stimulation, this warmth could provide a new metric for measuring the external influence, given that it is more sensitive than other indicators such as UV background. External stimulation of gas may also offer an alternative explanation for high excitation stages observed in some galaxies, and it could influence the formation of star clusters and the molecular gas itself.

We address the series reconstruction problem for permutations, which is a key issue arising in statistical applications, including probability theory, combinatorics, and random matrix theory. We consider a natural distance metric, the Hamming distance, to reconstruct permutations based on partial sum information. However, this distance leads to a non-truncated least squares problem with constraints, making its analytical solution complex. Nevertheless, we demonstrate that the Hamming distance between two permutations can be expressed in terms of the Kendall gamma diversity distance, providing a feasible approach to tackle the reconstruction problem via a direct analytical method. We further investigate the relationship between the Hamming distance and the Kendall gamma diversity distance as the number of sum observations increases, establishing its asymptotic properties. Moreover, we derive an estimator for the Hamming distance based on the normal distribution of the sample sums, and evaluate its performance through a simulation study. Finally, we explore extensions to the reconstruction problem for the Kendall gamma diversity distance under various constraints, and discuss potential applications, including ecology, genetics, and network analysis.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual binary black hole mergers in the future. Such detections are likely to occur for PTA signals resulting from binaries with substantial eccentricity due to their formation within the Milkyway's mass distribution. By implementing an efficient numerical approach, we have developed an analytical model for predicting PTA signals from merging binary systems with significant eccentricity. Our method allows for a precise match to numerical relativity simulations, achieving an accuracy of 2.2 x 10^-3 in metric fluctuations across the frequency range of interest, while maintaining a computational cost for signal generation at each frequency bin of approximately 0.75 ms. We have further tested the robustness of our approach under variations in the parameters of both the binary system and the PTA observatory, and found that our model's performance remains consistent. Our developed model is an essential tool for assigning physical meanings to future PTA detections, and we advocate for incorporating similar numerical techniques in the analysis of actual data sets.

We introduce a novel method called ASEP velocity procedure, which takes a random walk model as input and outputs another random walk model based on asymptotic behavior in the limit as time tends to infinity. This output model has a well-defined velocity that is extracted from the limit distribution of the original model's position. We demonstrate the ASEP velocity procedure's effects on three distinct input models by examining their resulting velocity distributions. Specifically, the plastic flow model, the nonlinear fractional Brownian motion model, and the correlated random walk model serve as our test cases. Notably, the plastic flow model and the nonlinear fractional Brownian motion model converge to the same velocity distribution when both are scaled by their respective variances, whereas the correlated random walk model yields distinct velocity distributions based on its correlation parameter.

Our analysis compares and contrasts different mathematical approaches used to model the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic surge. We examine various methods, including differential equation-based models, network models, super-spreader events, and hybrid combinations of these frameworks. By highlighting both successful predictions and significant failures of individual models, we aim to identify key factors that influence the accuracy of these models and their ability to simulate real-world outcomes. We also explore the potential drawbacks of certain methods and strategies, in addition to analyzing established results from model applications. Our study focuses on models related to pandemic surge patterns and does not delve into epidemic control strategies or other uses of these models.

We have theoretically analyzed a novel phenomenon called particle-molecule transformation, where a spinless particle collides with two identical spin-1/2 fermions and results in the creation of a molecule and an extra particle of the same type and properties. This process is broken down into two possible paths: a two-body recombination where two spinless fermions become a molecule, and a third fermion is created from the vacuum. Alternatively, three spin-1/2 fermions can collide and yield a molecule and an extra fermion. This phenomenon has been predicted in research, but detecting it has proven challenging due to the need for high-intensity light that simultaneously creates molecules and additional particles from the vacuum. However, if we use a specific beam shape, specifically a Gaussian beam with overlapping foci, we can observe the particle-molecule transformation phenomenon, even in situations with high intensities. Notably, this specific beam shape causes three-body recombination to prefer the creation of two spin-1/2 fermions over a single molecule, a phenomenon called "particle-molecule spinor phase separation". This phenomenon can be observed in systems like ultra-cold atomic gases, where it can lead to the formation of distinct phases based on location, simply by shifting the foci relative to each other.

This paper proposes an improved model of nucleotide storage that combines hierarchical data structures and a publishing system. Initially, we review existing methods for storing hierarchical data and publishing updates in nucleotide storage. However, we identify limitations in these approaches, specifically the risk of incorrect hierarchy reconstruction and insufficient guidelines for determining the ideal published update size. To address these challenges, we offer specific recommendations for encoding hierarchical data and a published update size calculation. These proposals are demonstrated to enhance hierarchy reconstruction accuracy and reduce the required published update size. Moreover, we explore a potential implementation of this model using synthetic data.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, traditional numerical methods require significant computational effort and are often too slow for real-time use. In contrast, the proposed SWFNet model utilizes a shallow water equations-based design and delivers superior performance on river flow velocity predictions. Furthermore, it surpasses the performance of traditional methods in terms of computational speed, being capable of achieving real-time predictions. In addition to its applicability to river flow velocity predictions, the model's solver-based design enables it to be utilized for solving shallow water equations directly. The code for SFWNet is publicly accessible at https://github.com/Qianhewu/SWFNet.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. This research presents a novel technique for automatically determining optimal exposure settings for smartphone images by leveraging the camera's inherent characteristics. Furthermore, an innovative method called weighted fusion is introduced to combine images captured at different exposure levels. This approach, compared to existing HDR techniques, takes into account the unique sensor characteristics, signal processing, and image capture behavior. As a result, the proposed technique outperforms current HDR methods in terms of image quality assessment, as demonstrated in the study's experiments.

In this talk, newly-integrated researchers in the field of causal learning discuss essential aspects that they believe anyone working with causal neural models should know. Speaking from their own recent experiences, they highlight important concepts, techniques, and considerations related to causal neural models, including counterfactual definitions, identification conditions, and treatment effects estimation. They also address related statistical topics, such as regularization, optimization, and validation, as well as important details about dataset creation and experimental design. With a focus on making this information accessible to a broad audience, they aim to help both seasoned experts and those just starting in the field to navigate the world of causal neural learning.

This note presents a new category of map functions called oriented map functions, which includes oriented bundle map functions as a subset. Building on the research of Madsen-McGaugh, it is proven that in certain cases, oriented map functions are stable under a specific type of variation, known as homotopy equivalences, if they are true embeddings. This phenomenon is reflected in a particular theorem called the oriented b-principle, which is a modification of the standard b-principle for map functions. The oriented b-principle can be viewed as a variation of the standard b-principle that includes the capacity to accommodate certain types of oriented surface embeddings. The proof of the oriented Madsen-McGaugh conjecture is a direct consequence of the oriented b-principle, and it is further demonstrated that the oriented b-principle leads to the convergence of a subsequence of certain scaled versions of minimally oriented surface embeddings, a result known as the weak convergence of a subsequence of these scaled embeddings. The research described is presented in three separate sections, each covering a distinct aspect of the topic. The first section discusses the development of oriented map functions and provides a stability criterion for them. The second section presents the oriented b-principle and examines its applications, including the stability of oriented bundle map functions and a subsequence convergence of scaled surface embeddings. This study compares the efficiency of various multilevel finite element methods
for solving a cardiac mechanics problem, particularly focusing on large-deformation
elastic models with discontiuous material properties. A key aspect analyzed
was how different methods handled mesh sizes in relation to tissue instability,
particularly in areas with fibrous tissues. Computational simulations were conducted
on a human heart model utilizing both quasi-linear and quasi-nonlinear methods,
and evaluated for accuracy, convergence, and computational costs. The study examined
various techniques for defining material properties and stability boundaries,
and explored the implications of these choices on computational results. Overall,
the study found that while there were several multilevel methods available, there
was limited consideration of the biological characteristics of the heart, such as
fibrous tissues, in existing literature.

We investigate a novel model of random permeability changes, which drives a stochastic diffusion process and causes it to exhibit anomalous diffusion characteristics, specifically super- and subdiffusion. The probability distributions of this model are found to match those of other, fundamentally different models that generate power-law distribution functions, thereby providing a new explanation for these distributions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this model can be applied to describe the motion of particles within porous media by modifying Darcy's law, and it includes previous laws as special cases.

A fundamental model has been developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interaction dynamics between an arbitrary system and optical resonators, based on their mode-specific alignment. The model, which takes into consideration both near-field interaction via electric polarization and far-field interaction via radiation, utilizes an all-encompassing mode interaction coefficient "g" to capture linear interaction dynamics and a mode-dependent second-order susceptibility "χ" to capture Kerr nonlinear interaction dynamics. By applying this model to a wide range of scenarios, including dielectric wavesguides, microresonators, photonic crystals, and dielectric surfaces, its versatility and utility in describing both linear and nonlinear interaction dynamics is demonstrated. Furthermore, it is shown that it can serve as a bridge between linear perturbation theory and variational perturbation theory in the case of weak Kerr nonlinearity.

A proposed new method utilizes GRNN and GAN models to enhance the resolution of turbulent flow images captured at various Reynolds numbers. The proposed technique involves creating a high-resolution simulation model based on a GAN and a low-resolution experimental model integrated through a GRNN, and then combining these models to achieve the desired high-resolution results. A representative example shows that this method can effectively improve the resolution of experimental chaotic flow images, capturing both the macroscopic surface features and the microscopic boundary layer regions. Comparative studies using PSNR and SSIM metrics also highlight the proposed method's superiority over alternative approaches, demonstrating notable gains of 26.7% and 53.5% in PSNR and SSIM, respectively.

For large language models like T0 and XL-T small-scale evaluation datasets are insufficient for accurately gauging model performance, due to limited testing breadth. Our proposed assessment framework, L2Explorer, tackles this issue to enable perpetual reinforcement learning and rigorous model evaluation. L2Explorer consists of an endless stream of evaluation tasks sourced from crowdsourcing, whose participants assess language generation tasks. We connect previously disconnected evaluation tasks to ensure continuous learning for models like T0 and XL-T small-size models. Our research demonstrates that using L2Explorer leads to significant improvements in tasks like machine translation and summarization, depending on the evaluation metric used. Interestingly, larger models like T0 Perform and XL-T Large sometimes perform worse on new, unseen data due to overfitting, as seen in evaluations of human readability and coherence. Our code and crowdsourcing tools for L2Explorer are available at https://github.com/nytng/L2Explorer.

The automatic detection of security breaches in business processes is a critical issue with various important implications, given the ever-increasing complexity and scale of processes. To address this challenge, our innovative method employs a declarative process representation that enables automatic identification of relevant data, as well as a sound and complete procedure for checking conditions against incoming events. By separating the process model from the environment, our approach allows for both rigorous analysis of the process and learning from observed patterns of the environment. Following an initial prototype implementation, our approach has been put into practice by a major financial institution as part of their ongoing process improvement efforts.

This research focuses on the parameter space Pkr of Krichever--Kac differential equations, which is obtained by identifying parameters that result in isospectral systems. The algebraic aspect of Pkr is explored through applications of algebraic geometry, specifically by constructing a rational map from the base space of a specific vector bundle to the Grassmannian Gr(3,6) via the Berkovich approach. Conversely, the analytical aspect of Pkr is studied within the framework of analytic geometry, which provides an abstract representation of Pkr as the compactification of a parameter space defined by analytic equations. A comparative analysis of these two representations reveals that they are equivalent and are based on the same geometric properties.

We investigated the relationship between maximum star formation rate (SFR) and stellar mass ($M_\omega$) in a database of 22,697 galaxies. We found that the existing break in the $M_\omega$-SFR ratio at $\log M_\omega \approx 10.2$ may be influenced by bulge dominance, as it is narrowed when bulge contributions are accounted for. Using a non-parametric regression technique, we discovered that the peak in SFR at higher masses could be explained by the presence of ancient, low-mass bulges with sufficient structural energy to prevent star formation from accelerating. Instead, we observe a turning point in $M_\omega$-SFR ratios when bulge masses fall into the range of giant bulges or pseudo-bulges, with $M_\omega$ spanning approximately $10.4 < \log M_\omega < 11.4$. This suggests that bulge formation marks the point at which star formation slows in more massive galaxies.

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news headlines using multiple languages. A common issue
with machine learning models is that they perform poorly for minority language
data due to significant classification errors. To overcome this challenge, a new
approach is proposed that utilizes a mixed set of languages for model training,
enabling the application to multiple languages with a single trained model.
Experimental evaluations in a massive dataset comprising seven languages,
with a significant amount of data available for three of them, demonstrate this
method's effectiveness compared to conventional approaches.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with diagnostic significance that can be difficult for humans to quantify.  With the emergence of X-ray-based automated systems for detecting COVID-19, it is crucial to investigate potential links between existing ICU admission criteria and X-ray features.  This criterion, which includes respiratory failure, cardiovascular conditions, age, and other factors, may provide a framework for interpreting the patterns evident in COVID-19 X-ray images.  Our analysis indicates that there are distinct differences in X-ray image characteristics based on the presence or absence of certain ICU admission criteria.  In particular, patients with severe COVID-19 cases who require ICU admission tend to exhibit specific X-ray features such as solid opacities, particular distribution patterns, and other less distinct characteristics.  Our proposed classification system incorporates these X-ray features in order to facilitate automatic COVID-19 severity assessment.  Our approach involves training multiple classification models, including traditional logistic regression and decision trees, as well as deep learning techniques such as CNN and transformer networks, using datasets derived from real-world clinical data.  These models can potentially be used for both low-risk patient diagnosis and to identify patients requiring ICU admission.

Given a bundle X → B with structure map π, we construct the global simplicial bundle ΣX → ΣB, using the simplicial structure of the mapping space SimpN∗(X) → SimpN∗(B). We prove that the simplicial structure of the mapping space SimpN∗(X) → SimpN∗(B) is compatible with the bundle properties, specifically it makes SimpN∗(X) a bundle over SimpN∗(B) for each N. Furthermore, we show that using the simplicial structure of the mapping space SimpN∗(X) → SimpN∗(B) is equivalent to using the simplicial bundle ΣX → ΣB with structure maps πN : ΣN(X) → ΣN(B) for each N.

The problem of erroneous positives in visual association detection persists, hindering the development of reliable and precise methods. This challenge stems from the asymmetric nature of this task, where the output space is substantially larger than the input, making it difficult to achieve balanced precision and recall. In an effort to address this issue, we present a novel technique that incorporates a soft view of the output feature space through a set of distinct bases, enabling effective dimensionality reduction without a fixed upper limit. This dynamic approach allows for the elimination of unnecessary positives and a focus on the most critical associations. In experiments conducted on the CUB-200-2011 dataset, our method exceeded the performance of existing techniques in terms of mean average precision by 3.5%, showcasing its potential for handling the issue of erroneous positives.

We've performed super-high resolution simulations of a young galaxy cluster for three centuries, yielding detailed models of multiple uneven stellar disks. These disks, free from significant merger activity, have distinct bulge formations due to internal forces, and our research reveals that an unequal distribution of accretion and gas consumption leads to the development of bulges. As matter accumulates at the cluster's center, the main response is not a massive black hole but rather an excessively dense star cluster. Furthermore, we observe sustained star formation in disk edges and an unusual buildup in the galaxy's core, affecting its overall structure over time.

Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (2700 m above sea level) reveal the presence of high-energy protons that lasted for two days following the massive solar flare on November 7, 2004. This observation took place during a special solar event characterized by a powerful X20 class flare and a massive CME, resulting in significant disruption to Earth's magnetic field and atmosphere. High-altitude observations of this phenomenon allowed our team to study the effects of solar energy on the upper atmosphere across different latitudes and to detect signs of composition change in high-energy particles. Further analysis of these findings was made possible by utilizing detailed records of solar neutrons obtained from the BeppoSaxon space telescope.

This paper presents an in-depth analysis of a notable phenomenon observed during the spin-up of KW Dor, an eccentric binary star. Our new measurements of KW Dor's rotation speed reveal a unexpected decrease in its rate, counter to expectations based on its eccentric orbit. This slowdown is particularly pronounced at the star's periastron, where we find a notable increase in broad-band flux that cannot be attributed to any known astrophysical process. Although some researchers suggest this increase in flux could be caused by planetary absorption, our study finds this hypothesis unlikely. Instead, we propose an alternative explanation involving the reduction of KW Dor's angular momentum due to its eccentric orbit, which could have far-reaching implications for our understanding of angular momentum in binary systems.

Due to the rapid dissemination of information on social media, fake news can spread quickly, and detecting it has become an urgent task. Deep learning models have made significant progress in fake news detection, but most current approaches rely on large amounts of labeled data, making them less practical for real-world applications. Additionally, the high frequency of new fake news means that traditional detection methods based on labeled data can struggle to perform well, especially in the early stages of their deployment. This paper proposes a novel framework called Multimodal Meta Counterfactual CPN (MMCCPN) for counterfactual fake news detection, considering the diversity of fake news and user perspectives. This framework leverages user feedback in the meta-training process to create a flexible system that can efficiently learn the underlying structure of fake news. For evaluation, we introduce a new metric called the average counterfactual accuracy, which assesses the performance of MMCCPN on unseen fake news articles. Our results show that MMCCPN significantly outperforms existing deep learning-based baselines in multiple evaluation settings, especially when there is limited label information.

This research paper examines a recurring transport equation with variables in two spaces and the effect of it having multiple solutions. The recurring framework is characterized by an iterative method that advances with time $t$ and maps the solution from time $s$ to time $s+t$, taking into account the random movements of the spaces' velocities. The velocities' properties take the form of random movements taking place within a bounded domain in $\mathbb{R}^d$, with occasional discontinuities in time $t$. Taking these properties into account, we prove that the recurring transport equation has multiple solutions for certain initial conditions, demonstrating its uniqueness only when the velocities over time $t$ are smooth. The proof involves a new result about the recurring continuity equation with missing data, where we establish the existing solution to be unique when the velocities' movements lie within a compact set in the space of random movements.

A diverse array of designs that incorporate Golay complementary sequences in multiple phases has been explored. These diverse designs, structured around phase-defined Golay complementary arrays, are distinguished by their complementary pairings that span across different phases. It has been demonstrated that in both binary and non-binary settings, phase-defined Golay complementary arrays can be incorporated into designs that employ matrix folding, cyclic, and dichotic structures. Moreover, these diverse designs can be characterized by their autodotcomplementary and bispectrally complementary properties. It has been further shown that non-binary phase-defined Golay complementary arrays can be constructed using quadratic generalizations of dichotic structures and matrix folding, thereby expanding the existing arrays in both binary and non-binary contexts.

Quantum spin transfer between silicon surface states and molecular states linked to surface functionalization has been investigated. It was found that valley interaction, which causes a shift in energy, can be influenced by spin transfer and binding energy of molecules on the silicon surface. This effect varies depending on the valley and a specific pattern of transfer is predicted, which could be identified using scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy. The research demonstrates the potential for controlling and measuring spin transfer and valley interaction with silicon-based quantum technologies.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interconnected components typically follow nonlinear dynamics that can lead to devastating consequences due to the sudden failure of specific parts. To mitigate these effects, researchers focus on understanding and analyzing these complex networks, often utilizing differential equations to model their dynamics. However, solving these equations is fraught with challenges, especially when the systems are large. A novel, two-step approach has been proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the architecture of the network is learned using artificial neural networks, and in a second step, the dynamics are determined using the known architecture. This proposed method eliminates the need to directly solve the differential equations and allows the use of nonlinear neural networks to model the dynamics. Furthermore, this method enables the use of graph neural networks to learn the architecture and dynamics of the system from raw data. We have implemented and tested this method on simple and complex networks and presented its application to learning the architecture and dynamics of a specific system from limited, raw data.

The Euler-Poincaré characteristic of a topological space is a long-established concept that can be computed using various methods. In the context of stable homotopy theory, it can be determined using the Euler characteristic of the cohomology ring, and this property extends to certain constructions within the category of spectra. By examining the partition poset, a partially ordered set that arises in the context of modular forms and exercise a profound impact on Kummer's criterion for divisibility, we can derive a formula to calculate the Euler characteristic of this space. Furthermore, this formula can be applied to evaluate the Euler characteristic of a specific spectrum called the modular forms spectrum, and it also provides an alternative derivation of the Euler characteristic of the K-theory spectrum for a specific space.

A cutting-edge medical technology has been developed to assist neurosurgeons in identifying and avoiding critical brain areas during surgical procedures, such as removing tumors. This technology, known as cerebral lesion prediction models, uses advanced mathematical models to analyze patient data and predict areas of damage, but it requires significant training data, a difficult task, given the limited information available before surgery. To address this challenge, a novel approach has been developed that uses real-world predicted lesion data in a creative way to expand the dataset further, thereby providing more accurate results to neurosurgeons. This approach, called the progressive adversarial variational auto-encoder, utilizes a unique combination of artificial intelligence techniques to accurately predict areas of damage by expanding the limited training data, and has been applied to create an advanced model that predicts areas of damage due to arteriovenous malformations, a type of brain blood vessel disorder.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the compilation process, the GP 2 compiler was upgraded to utilise a more advanced matching algorithm for rooted rules, leading to a significant reduction in compilation time. Additionally, the upgraded compiler is capable of providing valuable debugging information following compilation.

In recent years, attribute extraction from text has gained significant interest, and a number of approaches have been explored to achieve this task using contrastive learning methods. Although significant progress has been observed, there is still room for improvement, especially when it comes to scaling up to large attribute sets. Currently, most techniques construct separate pairs for each attribute, which can lead to pair size issues as the attribute set expands. In contrast, this paper presents a novel unified structure that creates a single set of attributes without pairing, facilitating efficient large-scale learning. The proposed structure supports both supervised and semi-supervised learning techniques and is particularly effective in reducing pair size expenses as it leverages the contrastive learning capability to differentiate between attributes by analyzing the overall distribution. Experimental evaluations conducted on large attribute sets demonstrated the efficacy of this structure, surpassing the performance of existing state-of-the-art methods even under significant pair size expenses.

We have identified a new class of graph properties that we call "twisted wreath composition," which builds upon existing concepts of graph composition and Cartesian products. This property allows us to generate a diverse range of complex-lookings star networks, many of which have never been documented previously. Specifically, we show that there are infinitely many twisted wreath type star networks that have a unique structural characteristic - their connected components are connected via distinct paths. We achieve this diverse output by establishing a formula for calculating the order of twisted wreath type star networks, and we find that it includes many previously unidentified networks as special cases.

Working with categorical data in model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its usefulness in handling categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing the Lasso on the obtained features. This strategy enables incorporation of external knowledge easily, such as linking categories together, which can be utilized to define groups of variables for selection and sparsity induction. We also provide an algorithm to efficiently implement this method and conduct an empirical analysis to demonstrate its effectiveness.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance in various tasks, surpassing the expertise of many human professionals, including experienced analysts (2020). Nonetheless, the speed at which the world changes necessitates continuous expertise updates, making it essential to explore methods for efficiently augmenting these models with new, previously unknown information, incorporating multiple complex sources, diverse in format and content. In response to this challenge, we present a novel approach, Structured Insight Infusion for Large Language Models (SKILL), capable of incorporating multiple unstructured text sources into a strong base LLM model. SKILL processes unstructured input for analysis, infusing the model with structured knowledge that can be employed for subsequent tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by incorporating unstructured COVID-19 research summaries into BART, leading to a 12% improvement in question-answering performance and the inclusion of unstructured industry expert reports into DeepMind's TTRF-S Imagination Model results in a 5% improvement in question-answering performance.

Achieving a seamless visual experience with mapping applications requires the efficient display of lines on display devices. Since line connections are often displayed in the form of connected segments, there's a common practice of rendering adjacent segments close to each other. This rendering approach can cause adjacent segments to intersect incorrectly due to the imprecisions inherent in digital devices, compounded by the line connection algorithm's limited precision. This paper addresses this issue by introducing a novel anti-aliasing technique specifically designed to render line connections on vector maps. By developing this technique, we've reduced the frequency of incorrect line connections and crosspoints, and have measured a significant decrease in rendering time. This reduction in rendering time and decreased rendering time in our example scenario was calculated as a 5.8% decrease in rendering time. This anti-aliasing technique can be applied to various line connections in mapping applications.

For single-channel speech enhancement in noisy environments, a system with two outputs is desired - one for each microphone signal with minimal noise, and an integrated output representing the enhanced speech signal. To achieve this, we propose the Dual-Path Convolutional Recurrent Network (DPCRN) architecture, comprising two separate networks working in conjunction to optimize separate microphone signals and then combine them. The proposed DPCRN architecture consists of two identical networks mirror-imaging each other, each tailored for single-channel speech enhancement tasks. These networks feed posterior mask estimates back to themselves through a recurrent connection to reduce noise. We train two DPCRN networks, each for different microphone signals, and then fuse them using a deep convolutional network to obtain the final enhanced speech signal. Experimentation with a widely-used dataset under various noisy conditions shows the proposed DPCRN architecture outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in various evaluation metrics.

Recently introduced multi-fluid modeling has promised enhanced simulation capabilities for atmospheric circulation, relying on the assumption that defined fluid components behave according to established laws. To evaluate this approach, a simple one-column two-fluid model was developed to simulate both vertically stable and unstable atmospheric conditions. By adjusting multiple variable parameters, the model successfully replicated the characteristics of both conditions. Furthermore, the model was used to investigate the underlying causes of unstable atmospheric situations, revealing that the behavior near which stability is lost or gained, known as the transition point, depends critically on several factors, including temperature, moisture, and turbulence.

We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to determine when this unconnected system could truly become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become entangled with the others if its cavity is highly occupied, provided that it is connected to another cavity with a specific type of quantum characteristic. Additionally, we examine various conditional operations on the unconnected system's atom, including measurements, interactions with a second atom, and Jaynes-Cummings interactions, to gauge their effect on entanglement.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the (1+3)-dimensional Reissner-Nordstr\"om-Penrose non-linear charged AdS black hole. We examine the thermodynamics of this black hole within a shadow system, investigating how the radius and charge determine the shape of the shadow. A distinctive donut-shaped shadow emerges when the black hole has a certain capacity to hold charge, and this shape is affected by both the mass and the nonlinear interaction. We also determine the phase transition boundaries for this black hole based on its mass, charge, and the strength of the nonlinear interaction. These boundaries indicate that the black hole may undergo a phase transition from a small, charged state to a state with a stronger nonlinear interaction, doing so at a critical mass that is directly influenced by the AdS radius.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and beginning of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances.

360-degree virtual travel videos offer an immersive viewing experience but require significant storage resources and have high computational costs due to their high resolution and three-dimensional nature. To make this engaging content more accessible on limited mobile platforms, a method of predicting the viewport by analyzing video subtitles has been proposed. In this approach, a viewport is predicted as a sphere with its center corresponding to the user's viewing position and a radius representing the distance from the user to the video's point of interest. By tracking this sphere's size over time, a threshold is established to determine whether to reduce the video resolution or terminate the session. Experiments using two large datasets have shown that the predicted viewports are accurate and consistent with actual views taken by users. These findings are promising for the efficient delivery of 360-degree virtual travel videos on restricted mobile platforms.

Tensor network techniques, which leverage the concept of a local, efficient representation of states and operations, have been a successful tool for approximating complex many-body systems. Given the efficiency of the tensor network representation, especially with the development of the Vernon Veronese version of the variational renormalization group method, researchers can now accurately describe both thermal equilibrium and dynamic states using a compact and local description. Our new tensor network framework, characterized by a single physical or virtual bond, allows us to represent both thermal equilibrium and dynamic states using a local and efficient representation. This representation enables the efficient implementation of time-evolved conditions and the formation of thermal conditions through the use of a single unitary operator, ensuring that the represented state remains physical throughout the process. Our approach serves as a starting point for further developments, such as the incorporation of local conserved quantities or the inclusion of external fields.

Numerical methods for solving partial differential equations often involve approximating the effectiveness of a decoupling barrier. In various applications, including nonlinear wave equations and transport equations with non-local operators, such approximations play a crucial role in decoupling components of the solution and are therefore essential for the scheme's effectiveness. The approximate representation of the effectiveness operator is typically required to maintain a certain level of accuracy in different regions of the domain. In this paper, a new strategy for approximating the effectiveness operator is introduced, which is distinguished by its performance in scaling and its ability to maintain accuracy in the regime where the decoupling barrier is nearly broken. This approach is particularly useful for developing numerical schemes that can handle a wide range of cases, from the linear to the fully nonlinear, and includes applications such as transport equations with the Boltzmann operator and nonlinear wave equations with the Kac-Zubkov operator. The paper also demonstrates how this approximation can be used to create a numerical scheme for solving a specific transport equation, and provides an analysis of the scheme's stability and its ability to preserve the non-negative character of solutions.

The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's variance is being quantified, and calculations demonstrate how non-linear small-x saturation impacts the PDF's behavior, particularly in the case of deep-inelastic scattering at high energies, where a power law $xG \propto x^{1-\delta}$ applies, with $\delta \approx 0.6$ resulting from infrared renormalon and requiring further verification from better understood approaches.

We present a theoretical model for a unique nanoarray made of rectangular patches made of ferromagnetic material and gold, arranged in a two-dimensional structure. This model exhibits distinct optical properties that are sensitive to the direction of an external magnetic field, especially in the longitudinal plasmon resonance region. By adjusting the shape of the patches from rectangular to elliptical, we can alter the optical response to better match the characteristics of propagation and polarization modes in the lattice. This transformation allows for even more significant effects from the long-range plasmariton mode due to a greater difference in the optical response between no magnetic field and a high-strength field. Our findings demonstrate the potential of this nanoarray to serve as a multibit magnetic field sensor that can detect the orientation of its magnetic field with high accuracy.

Recent advancements in neural network training have been successful, yet there's still a gap in understanding how neural networks train and mislead. Despite being a critical issue, neural network training data in existing datasets is largely unaccounted for as target data. This lack of consideration affects the results of transfer learning, a key application of neural networks. To rectify this problem, we propose a novel framework for transferring knowledge from a neural network trained on a source dataset to a similar dataset without direct access to the target dataset. This framework operates in a decision-based black-box setting, where the neural network's internal characteristics are unknown, and it's only possible to query the network through classification tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework for transferring knowledge in several scenarios, including compressing models and enhancing robustness. Moreover, our approach is versatile enough to handle a wide range of datasets, including those with multiple classes. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/zwang84/zsbbff.

The study identifies possible signs of two rare occurrences, $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{(*0)} \bar{K}^0_S$, which have been hard to detect due to confusion with background from $B^0_s\to D^{(*0)} \bar{K}^0_S$ decay patterns. The research uses 63 pb$^{-1}$ of data collected by LHCb at a 7 TeV proton-proton collision facility. The likelihood of $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{(*0)} \bar{K}^0_S$ happening is calculated to be (3.0$\pm$0.5) $\times 10^{-5}$, indicating it could be a significant process. The study also highlights the importance of further investigation into $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{(*0)} \bar{K}^0_S$ with various observables and into $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0_S$ with specific $D^* $ polarization characteristics.

Given a module $R$ that is free from submodules having specific depths, determining the structure of its submodule lattice involves a clear understanding of its submodules, inferences about missing submodules, and the relationship between them. In this research, we demonstrate how to construct the lattice of $R$'s submodules using a graded ring $S$ with defined properties, which provides essential information about the missing submodules and their relationship. Furthermore, we show that the dimension of $S$ is equal to the depth of $R$, and both share a significant property. Additionally, we offer a concrete example to illustrate this method.

Understanding how agents learn from each other through observation is vital in creating successful collaborative systems. Typically, a learner requires the expert to demonstrate tasks multiple times to match the expert's performance, which isn't always practical due to time constraints and expertise availability. To address this challenge, we develop a new Co-Observation Learning algorithm, allowing the learner to pair with the expert for just two observations: once to understand the task and once to apply that understanding. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in various scenarios, showing it outperforms traditional learning methods using few demonstrations and other observation-based methods using many observations.

We introduce PAC codes as a new code category that combines the error-correction capabilities of classical codes and the privacy preservation of quantum codes. Based on a threshold principle, we determine the required density for efficient error correction and quantify a variable, known as the classical quantum boundary, to delimit efficient regions of PAC codes. Classical quantum boundary calculations are carried out for specific code types, including stationary states described by the Fock representation, Atkinson states, and states defined by single-qubit operators, both for specific orientations and general cases.

Using reinforcement learning post maximum likelihood estimation preprocessing can be effective in optimizing neural machine translation systems. Nonetheless, a significant issue with RL for NMT arises from the extensive action space resulting from the vocabulary size, which causes training to run into difficulties due to the vanishing exploration problem. Various solutions have been proposed to scale RL for NMT, including reducing the action space by utilizing multiple action sets or the vocabulary, establishing compact action sets through clustering, and selecting words based on the history of translation. In this paper, we propose introducing a simple yet effective method called Reorder-through-Masked LM (RML) that leverages masked LM to efficiently explore the action space without clustering or accessing the vocabulary. In RML, a mask-learn model is trained to predict the next word in a sequence by generating an output based on the input tokens except the target word. We can then determine the optimal action by selecting the word forecasted in the usual position in the predicted output. Experiments on widely-used datasets for RL for NMT demonstrate notable improvements, and our proposed method compares favorably to existing methods belonging to the two categories of scaling RL for NMT.

The study of open quantum systems under periodic driving forces is highly captivating, and the study of qubits under periodic driving in superconducting circuit systems is a specific and promising area of research. These systems, once implemented, will be extremely sensitive to the effects of driving and the dynamics of the system, due to their minute size. Consequently, they have the potential to serve as accurate standards for calculating physical and technical parameters in the development of future applications. The development of these standards is crucial for ensuring that developments stay on track and that future enhancements are made with a full comprehension of necessary improvements. We explore how certain recurring operators including differentiation and composition with the inverse of the vector retracement operator, act within the biharmonic hypersurfaces in a four-dimensional Euclidean space.

A rational number p/q, greater than 1, identifies two distinct collections of intervals if it falls within exactly one of the combined intervals, namely (0,1). It recognizes three distinct collections of intervals if it falls within two of the combined intervals, namely (0,1)\((1-p/q)$ and $ (p/q, 2)$. This paper explores the properties of a prime number 3, greater than 1, in relation to a set of intervals on the real line and develops formulas to calculate the sets' identifiable members. It also investigates how the sets' identifiable members change when the sets themselves change.

MongoDB, a popular NoSQL database, offers a suite of transactions known as multi-document transactions. These transactions enable users to conduct multiple operations across different documents in a single, all-or-nothing transaction. This development addresses key challenges with NoSQL databases, including the transactional integrity and consistency. However, implementing consistency through transactions comes with a price, including reduced system availability and performance drawbacks. Therefore, it is essential to validate the integrity of these transactions regularly. In response to the need for validating the integrity of MongoDB's transactions, we have designed and implemented an open-source tool called MiTChecker. MiTChecker evaluates the effectiveness of MongoDB's multi-document transactions in maintaining data consistency and identifying potential issues with the database's configuration or code. The tool can detect various problems, including inconsistent data resulting from transactions, incorrect use of read and write operations, and failed transactions due to versioning conflicts. By utilizing MiTChecker, developers can ensure the integrity of their data stored in MongoDB using multi-document transactions and reduce the risk of implementation errors. Additionally, the tool provides valuable feedback that can be used to improve MongoDB's transaction functionality.

Using the combinatorial definition of chromatic symmetric functions, we demonstrate that certain coefficients are always positive when expanding a specific set of symmetric functions. Additionally, our analysis connects these results to the inverse Kostka matrix, particularly highlighting a negative coefficient in the expansion of a particular symmetric function. This particular negative coefficient arises from the inverse Kostka matrix's non-positive properties along its main diagonal.

We have developed a novel type of complex geometric framework that is inspired by Lorenzian manifold concepts and incorporates triangle-based interactions between nodes. This method is particularly useful for describing intricate networks that consist of multiple small triangles. Our approach is closely related to a specific type of nonlinear Schrödinger equation known as the NLS-Lax pair equation. By applying our method to a specific nanoscale assembly model that involves mutual interactions between nodes, we are able to derive a new type of nonlinear Schrödinger equation with multiple components. Our results show that this model can exhibit diverse behavior, including spin reversal dynamics. Our approach is publicly available upon request.

An analysis of solar wind energy transfer was performed by applying a new method to data from four locations within the heliosphere, using data from far ultraviolet cameras and magnetometers. The new approach, known as extended two-stream model, incorporates both non-thermal electrons and plasma instabilities observed with the Solar Dynamics Observatory, allowing for a more accurate determination of the average energy of electrons. The results reveal that the solar wind carries 7.5 GW of energy flow towards Earth, with an associated electron energy flux of 1.8 x 10^-3 W/m^2. The energy transfer efficiency of the solar wind decreases at greater distances from the sun, from about 0.8 in the inner heliosphere to around 0.6 closer to Earth. The relationship between this decrease and the energy transfer efficiency of electrons and the solar wind energy transfer is unclear and requires further investigation.

To enhance communication, including bonding and conciliation, speech emotion recognition (SER) is being explored for potential uses in multiple areas. Despite significant progress made so far, existing models face two significant challenges. First, they require large amounts of labeled data for training and accuracy, as well as substantial expertise and resources to set up and maintain. Second, they struggle to adapt to new domains with limited data, a common issue in domain adaptation. This study addresses both issues by introducing a systematic approach to facilitate both domain adaptation and low-data training for a deep reinforcement learning-based SER model. The proposed method involves multiple innovations. Firstly, the paper develops a speech emotion reinforcement learning framework, which utilizes a two-step process to convert intuitive emotional labels into more useful guide signals. Secondly, the paper incorporates an entropic regularization term and employs a domain-adaptive loss function to adapt to new domains with minimal data. To validate the proposed method, the study conducts comprehensive experiments on two datasets using three evaluation metrics. The results show that the proposed model performs better than the existing state-of-the-art models in both domain adaptation and low-data learning settings.

Researchers studying high-energy particle physics have a strong interest in enterring an extremely high-density state deep within dense matter, yet this density is difficult to achieve in laboratory settings. However, such conditions can be easily achieved in the heart of dense stars. Despite this, there is a lack of theoretical understanding of dense matter's properties at these high densities. To address this, we are conducting a series of investigations into the dynamics of dense stars, focusing on their ability to develop rapid rotation through the absorption of massive objects. During this process, a dense star may develop a sudden and intense shock wave if it has a specific composition of matter. We are examining how the speed of this shock wave changes in response to various factors, including the initial density of the star, its composition, its overall mass, and its rate of rotation. In the case of neutron stars, we are also comparing our findings to those from other studies, while also exploring the potential for these stars to release high-energy particles through the interaction of their shock waves with spherical voids or in a rapidly expanding cosmos.

Using $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ data, an investigation of the QCD approach to determine the $b$ quark mass is conducted, alternative methods of calculation are considered, and the shape of the hadron form factor involved is examined. Hays et al. initially established the shape of this form factor with an uncertainty of 4.3%. The proposed experiment aims to reduce this uncertainty by employing two different methods to extract the form factor shape and its associated error.
